title: Data Validation and Factory Methods
tagline: Where does "is this legal?" live?  One door in, one place the rules are written.
newIdea: A type should be **impossible to construct in an invalid state**
builtOn: Lesson 1.  Your dice are already immutable -- that is what makes today's move worth anything.
goals: Write a guard clause that refuses a bad value **where the mistake was made**, and say what validating late costs instead
Make a constructor private and expose factory methods, so that every caller comes through the rules
Write factories that **compose** -- each one calling the general factory and leaving the rules where they are
Choose between **throwing** and **returning false**, based on where the bad value came from

vocab.def: a check at the top of a method that refuses bad input and gets out immediately
something that is true about an object for its entire life, because the type guarantees it
an error that travels up the call stack looking for somebody who knows what to do about it
a static method that builds an object -- so construction can say what it is *for*, and can refuse
`TryParse(input, out result)` returning `bool`.  C#'s way of saying "this might fail, and failure here is Tuesday"

warmup: Last week you made dice that are fixed the moment they are built.  So how many moments are there, now, when a set of dice can be wrong?  Count them.  Then look at the museum in Scene 1 and decide which exhibit worries you most -- and be ready to argue about it, because the expensive one is probably the quiet one.

p: If a value can only ever be set while the object is being built, then the moment it is built is the **only** moment it can be wrong.
That is an enormous simplification and it came free with the decision you already made last lesson.  Today we stand on that one moment and put a door on it.

howItWorks.h: Loud failure is cheap.  Quiet wrongness is expensive.
p: Scene 1 builds eight sets of dice.  Some are refused.  Some roll happily.  One is accepted and then detonates.
The instinct is to say the crash is the worst one.  Look again.  The crash told you immediately, at the line where you made the mistake.  The `1d0` shipped.

Read the crash message when you get to it:  *'minValue' cannot be greater than maxValue.*  Everybody in this room can see those are somebody else's words.  That message came from inside `Random`.  Your bad value walked out of your type, into somebody else's code, and blew up there -- in their vocabulary, pointing at their variable names.
That is what validating late buys you.
**You may already know this one**, and if so you are ahead of the lesson.

"Consider static factory methods instead of constructors" is the opening item of *Effective Java*, and the reasons Bloch gives are the reasons here:  a factory has a name, it can refuse, and it is free to hand back an object that already exists.
So this is the same idea you have already met, and the language you know reached for it too.
bullets: What C# adds is `Dice.D20` -- a shared instance handed out by a factory, which is only safe because Lesson 1 made it unchangeable.  In Java you would be reaching for the same trick and worrying about the same thing.
The Java habit to actually drop is the parameterless constructor plus setters.  A private constructor ends that shape, and rightly so.

p: Open `Dice.cs` and look at the constructor.  It is **private**, and it trusts its three numbers completely.  It can afford that, because this file is the only place that can reach it.
Try writing `new Dice(0, 0)` in `Program.cs`.  The compiler rejects it.

code.label: The constructor, and the only things that can reach it

bullets: **Every one of them defers to `Of()`.** `Attack` is one line.  `TryParse` does string work and then hands off.
One door, one place the rules are written, and every caller through it.
A constructor gets **one** name and has to accept whatever it is given.  A factory gets as many names as your game has ideas -- and gets to refuse.

p: The split itself will be familiar -- it is roughly Java's checked versus unchecked exceptions, drawn along the same line:  is this the caller's mistake, or a thing that just happens?

The mechanism differs.  C# leaves every exception unchecked, so handling stays the caller's decision and the `throws` clause is absent entirely.  What C# reaches for is the **Try pattern**: a `bool` return plus an `out` parameter.
aside.code:
Java:  int n = Integer.parseInt(s);   // throws
C#:    int.TryParse(s, out var n)     // returns false
bullets: If you know `Optional<T>`, this is the same job done with a different tool -- and a noisier one.  `out` is genuinely awkward syntax; it is also everywhere in the standard library, so it is worth being fluent in.

p: Two different failures, two different answers.  The question to ask is **where did it come from**.

code.label: Same rules, two paths
code.body:
Dice.Of(0, 6)                              // I wrote this.  If it's wrong, that's a BUG.     -> throw
Dice.TryParse(whatThePlayerTyped, out var d)   // They wrote this.  If it's wrong, that's Tuesday. -> false

bullets: Bad value from **your own code** → **throw**.  Fail loudly, at the mistake.
Bad value from **a file, a player, a mod, a network** → **`TryParse`**.  Return `false` and carry on.
Both go through the same guards.  `TryParse` catches the refusal and turns it into an answer.
`out var dice` is a second thing the method hands back, alongside the `bool`.

p: A value can be wrong in two different ways, and the line between them is yours to draw.
bullets: **Formatting is noise.**  `" 2d6 "`, `"2D6"`, `"2d6"` are one claim typed by three people.  Clean it up quietly; everything meaningful survives.  (`TryParse` already does this for you.  Find the line.)
**Meaning is a claim.**  `"0d6"` says something false.  Refuse it.
Where does `"2 d 6"` go?  You and the person next to you will disagree, and you each need a reason.

howItWorks.h: Two forms for the limits, and why

p: Your fingers are going to type `public static const int` exactly once, because Java spells this `static final`.  C# will stop you with **CS0504** -- *the constant cannot be marked static* -- because a `const` is already static and saying so twice is one word too many.

The second form stands on its own, with the closest Java equivalent some way off.  `public static int MaxCount => 100;` is a **property**: it is recomputed every time it is read, which is why it needs the `static` keyword that a `const` carries on its own.
bullets: Java's naming convention would be `MAX_COUNT`.  C#'s is `MaxCount` -- PascalCase for everything public, constants included.

p: Look at the top of `Dice.cs`.  `MinSides` is a `const`.  The other three are `static` properties.  That is a claim about how permanent each number is.

code.label: The form is the documentation
code.body:
public const  int MinSides    = 2;      // STRUCTURAL - a die with fewer than two faces
                                        // to choose between, in this game or any other

public static int MaxCount    => 100;   // HOUSE RULES - this table's numbers.  Another
public static int MaxSides    => 1000;  // game picks different ones and is still
public static int MaxModifier => 20;    // playing with dice

bullets: A `const` is **already** `static`.  You reach it as `Dice.MinSides`, straight off the type.  If you learned `static final` somewhere else, your fingers will try `public static const` exactly once -- that is **CS0504**.
`public static int MaxCount => 100;` is a **property**.  It is computed each time it is asked for, which is why it *needs* the `static` keyword that a `const` carries on its own.

Only a `const` can appear in a pattern.  The guards could have been written as `count is >= 1 and <= MaxCount`, which is idiomatic modern C#. A pattern requires a `const`, and `MaxCount` is a property.  Try it and read **CS9135**.
Go break that last one on purpose.  Knowing which compiler errors are real design rules and which are just syntax is worth five minutes.

steps: Run `Course/starters/Lesson02_ValidationAndFactories`.  `Program.cs` is a report card on your `Dice` type -- **leave it alone** until the very end.
Try writing `var d = new Dice(0, 0);` in `Program.cs`.  The compiler rejects it.  That is the whole design, in one error message.  Delete it and move on.

Read **Scene 1**.  For each exhibit marked `ROLLED`, finish this sentence:  *"Six months from now, this shows up as a bug report that says ______."* The one marked `ACCEPTED, THEN CRASHED` is a different kind of bad -- say how.
Inside `Of()`, `count` has a guard and `sides` is wide open.  Write one, right next to it, using `MinSides` and `MaxSides`.  Re-run:  three exhibits change.

`modifier` is wide open too.  Give it a rule using `MaxModifier`.  Decide for yourself whether a negative modifier is legal -- it is, but *how* negative?  Write down the reason for the number you pick.
Grow `TryParse` until Scene 2 loads what should load and refuses the rest.  Add a missing count first (`"d20"` means `"1d20"`), then a modifier (`"3d8+2"`, `"1d4-1"`).  Re-run after each.

Add three archetypes to `Dice` that your game would actually use.  **Make them call `Of()`** -- if you are re-typing a rule, you have gone wrong.  Look at how `Attack` and `AbilityScore` are one line each.

**Count what you touched.**  You wrote two rules, in one method.  Now list everything that got them for free:  `Attack`, `AbilityScore`, `ByName`, `Parse`, `TryParse`, and all six `Dice.D*` presets.  Every one of them stays silent about the limits.  That is what the private constructor bought you:  **one place to change your mind.**

code.label: The worked example - the count guard, already written
The Try pattern - one copy of every rule

makeItYours: **Open your `Card.cs` from Lesson 1** and do to it what we did to `Dice`.

**Break it on purpose first.**  Before writing a single guard, construct the five worst Cards your design allows.  A card missing its suit.  A rank of 47.  A rank of -3.  Print them.  Look at what your type was willing to build.
Sort each failure into **noise** (fix it quietly -- `"ace of spades"`, `"ACE OF SPADES"`, `" AS "`) or **a claim** (refuse it -- rank 47).  Say where you put the line.
**Make the constructor private.**  Then work out what factory methods your game actually wants.  `Card.Of(rank, suit)`?  `Card.AceOf(suit)`?
Give `Card` a `TryParse`.  `"AS"` is the ace of spades, `"10H"` the ten of hearts.  Then survive these:  `"2c"`, `" KS "`, `"1S"`, `"11H"`, `"ZZ"`, `""`, `"10"`.
Write a factory that hands back a **full standard deck**.  Fifty-two cards, each one distinct, the whole grid covered.  Prove it -- print the count.
challenge: Count how many of your own factory methods restate a rule in place of calling through to one place.  Every one that does is somewhere your future self can forget to update.  Fix them, then say how many you found.
flintHint: Good things to ask:  "what is the difference between throwing and returning false in C#?", "why does my static property fail in a pattern?", or "how do I write a TryParse method with an out parameter?" Tell it you are on Lesson 2 and that your constructor is private on purpose -- otherwise it will suggest you just make it public.

wrapup: Name one rule you wrote.  Is it protecting you from a bug in your code, or from bad data outside it?  Show me where it lives *because* of that.
assignmentTask: Give `Dice` the two rules it is missing, grow `TryParse` until the rulebook loads correctly, and then make your own `Card` impossible to build wrong.
assignmentDo: Add guards for `sides` and `modifier` inside `Of()`, and be able to say why that is the place for them.
Grow `TryParse` until Scene 2 loads `2d6  d20  3d8+2  1d4-1  4d6  2d6  1d20+3` and refuses everything else.
Add three factory archetypes that **call `Of()`** and leave the rules where they are.
In your own `Card.cs`: break it on purpose first, then make the constructor private and put every rule behind a factory.
Be ready to answer:  which of your rules protect against a **bug in your code**, and which against **bad data from outside it**?
submit: Your `Card.cs`, including the deck factory and its printed count.
The list of the five worst Cards you were able to build **before** you added guards.  Keep it -- that list is evidence.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Show that the compiler rejects `new Dice(...)` from outside the type, and say why that is the point.
Point at a guard and say whether it is catching my bug or somebody else's bad data.
Show `TryParse` handling `"d20"`, `"3d8+2"`, and `"1d4-1"`, and refusing `"0d6"` and `"twenty"`.
Show three archetypes that leave every rule to `Of()`.
Print 52 from my own deck factory, every card distinct.
standard: Make a type impossible to construct in an invalid state, using a private constructor and composing factory methods, and choose correctly between throwing and the Try pattern.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: Guards still to write, or the build is red.  **Next step:**  look at how the `count` guard inside `Of()` is written -- check the value, throw with a message naming the parameter, then get out.  Copy that shape for `sides`.  If you are getting **CS9135**, you tried to use `MaxSides` in a pattern; a pattern requires a `const` and this is a property, so write it as `sides < MinSides || sides > MaxSides` instead.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: `Of()` guards all three values, `TryParse` loads the seven valid lines and refuses the rest, and Scene 1's museum has been cleared of everything embarrassing.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and my own `Card` has a private constructor with every rule behind a factory, a working `TryParse`, and a deck factory that prints 52 -- and I can say which of my rules catch bugs and which catch bad data.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I went after something the lesson left open -- an enum-based rank that makes `"11H"` impossible to express, a `Result` type in place of exceptions, a factory that composes so cleanly a new archetype is one line, or a real argument about where `"2 d 6"` belongs that I can defend from both sides.

thinking: In two or three sentences:  name one rule you wrote and say whether it protects against a bug in your code or bad data from outside it.  Then say how many places in your `Card` a rule is written down -- and whether that number is the one you want.

p: Open with the callback, because it makes the whole style cohere:  "Last week you made dice that are fixed the moment they are built.  So how many moments are there, now, when a set of dice can be wrong?"
One.  The moment it is built.  That is an enormous simplification and it came free with the decision they already made.  Today we put a door on that moment.

This is also the honest reason the private constructor is worth its ceremony.  Lesson 1 is what gives it teeth, since a locked constructor means something only when everything after construction is sealed too.
Show the `count` guard inside `Of()` -- already written.  Name it.  Point at the three parts of the exception:  which parameter, what value, what the rule is.
Contrast with the `Random` message they just read in Scene 1:  "An error message is written for the person who has to fix it.  Write it for them."

di.h: One door -- the move of the lesson
p: Have them try `var d = new Dice(0, 0);` in Program.cs.  The compiler rejects it.

"So how did Scene 1 make dice at all?" Put the list of factories on the board and ask what they have in common.  Then the payoff, which you want THEM to say:  "How many places do you have to write the rule that dice need at least one die?"

One.  The private constructor is what makes that guarantee real, because the compiler enforces it.  Politeness and convention would leave it optional.  It is the compiler refusing to let anybody route around `Of()`.
Contrast explicitly:  a constructor gets ONE name and must accept what it is given; a factory gets as many names as the game has ideas, and can refuse.
Show `TryParse` in the source ending with a try/catch around `Of()`.  Same rules, both paths, one copy.  That is the thing to point at.
The `out` parameter is new to most of them.  One sentence:  "a second thing the method hands back, alongside the bool." Stop there.

di.h: Why the longhand constructor here? -- have the answer ready
p: Somebody will ask where the terse positional form went.  Two reasons, and the second is the one that matters.
Mechanically:  a primary constructor is always public in C#, and `record Dice private(...)` is a parse error, CS1514.  You choose a primary constructor or a private constructor.

Really:  a primary constructor is a PUBLIC front door with open space where a rule would go.  That suits a type whose data stands on its own perfectly well.  A save-file record, a parsed config line, a message shape.  Those are DTOs, and gating one behind a factory would be ceremony guarding an empty room.

The split they should end up with:  **has invariants to protect** → private ctor + factory.  **Is a shape, data alone** → primary constructor.  Primary constructors arrive with DTOs, post-fork, wherever save/load lands.  Hold them back here.

guided: Everyone runs the starter first.  Scene 1 is the hook and it needs to land before any instruction.
Have the whole room try `new Dice(0, 0)` and fail to compile.  Ten seconds, and it makes the private constructor something they felt.
Steps 4 and 5 individually.  Circulate -- the most common miss is writing the guard as a pattern and hitting CS9135.
Step 6 is the longest and it is Meeting B. Have them run Scene 2 after each sub-step, one change at a time.
Step 8, the counting exercise, as a whole class.  Protect it -- see notes.
Release to Cards for the back half of Meeting B. The deck factory is what most will need help SCOPING; the writing comes easily.
pitfalls: **Guards written as patterns** -- `sides is >= MinSides and <= MaxSides` -- producing CS9135.  This is a good error to hit.  The limits are properties, and a pattern requires a `const` to appear in a pattern.  Let them read it before you explain it.
**New archetypes written as `new Dice(...)`,** which the compiler now rejects.  The error IS the lesson; point at it.  They must go through `Of()`.
**Archetypes that re-check a limit "just to be safe."** Ask what happens when the limit changes.  Two copies of a rule is one copy plus a future bug.
**`TryParse` handling the modifier BEFORE the split,** so `"1d4-1"` splits on `'d'` into `"1"` and `"4-1"`.  Have them print `text` at each stage.
`IndexOf('-')` where `LastIndexOfAny` belongs -- works until something has a negative count.  Let it break; the error teaches it faster than you can.

**try/catch everywhere,** because an exception feels like a crash they should prevent.  Push back once, clearly:  catching an exception you are powerless to fix is worse than letting it through -- it hides the report and leaves the bug where it was.
Deck factory built with nested loops over hard-coded string arrays.  Works fine.  Ask what happens when a rank gets misspelled, and let that push them toward enums if they have yet to go there.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: Any specific rule, correctly sorted.  The distinction to listen for:  a rule catching a programmer error should throw and live in `Of()`; a rule catching bad external data should be the `TryParse` path that catches that throw.  A student who says "both, it's the same rule" has actually got it -- there IS only one copy, and the two paths differ only in what they do with the refusal.
notes: **Pacing.**  Meeting A: 7 warm-up / 13 instruction / 22 guided (steps 1-5) / 5 wrap.  Meeting B: 5 recap / 15 guided (steps 6-8) / 25 Cards / 5 wrap.

**The thing to protect is step 8,** the counting exercise.  Two rules, eleven call sites, zero duplication.  Skip it and "make the constructor private" reads as ceremony somebody imposed on them.  With it, it reads as the thing that made the counting come out that way.

**Two arguments to leave open.**  First:  is `"2 d 6"` the same claim as `"2d6"`?  Genuinely arguable -- whitespace inside a token stands on different footing from whitespace around it.  Second:  is `1d20-50` valid?  The honest answer is that it is perfectly good dice notation and a terrible game rule, so the check belongs somewhere that knows about the game -- a layer still to come.  That layer is Lesson 3, and Lesson 3 is built to land exactly there.

If a student gets to "that belongs to the game, and the dice type is the wrong place for it," write their name down.  That is the whole arc of the next lesson arriving a week early, from a student, which is worth more than anything you can say.
The same shape appears in Cards immediately:  is a rank of 11 invalid, or is it a Jack?  Depends on the game.  Let them find it.

**A hole you should know about and leave alone.**  A record still supports `with` from outside the type, and `with` sidesteps your factory -- `Dice.D20 with { Sides = 0 }` would sail straight past `Of()`.  `with` waits for a later lesson by design, so students will walk past this on their own.  If a sharp student finds it, that is a real discovery:  they have found the one door the factory leaves open, and reconciling those two is exactly why `with` gets its own lesson later, alongside DTOs.  Leave it be -- a hole a student can see is the only kind worth teaching.

**If they finish early:**  `GameData/Items/Item.cs` in the finished game validates by NORMALIZING -- negative weight becomes zero, an empty name becomes "Unknown Item", every value coerces, and construction stays wide open at all.  That is the opposite call from the one they just made.  Ask which is right.  (Both are.  It depends on whether a wrong item should stop the game.  It should let the player keep going -- a player with a weird item keeps playing.  A wrong die probably should, because every number after it is nonsense.)
